Foreword
Why did you buy this game?
Thank you for your purchase, by the way. Seriously though, what struck you?
The beautiful art? The unending pursuit to own every piece of Stargate franchise
merchandise? An impulse buy?
I would wager your love of Stargate. Tap every fourth person, and they'll likely say,
"That one with MacGyver?" The fifth or sixth person you reach out to might say, "I
saw it in the theatres." But before you hit eighth or ninth, you'll find someone who's
seen more than a few episodes. And definitely by the twelfth, I'll wager you'll find
a fan. That's something beautiful.
So why do you love the show? Before you make a character in this new Stargate SG-1
Roleplaying Game, spend time on that question. The adventure? The exploration?
The romance? The nice thing about Stargate SG-1, and this is true of most smart
science fiction, is that you can passively experience it while doing the dishes, or you
can invite almost every episode to "hold a mirror" to you and your preconceptions
about countless topics.
Despite being set in the here-and-now, the Stargate itself gives us not only that
vehicle for exploration both into outer space, but also into the inner space of our
own lives. Can the actions of one person light a spark that ignites action in others,
like with Teal'c? Can family learn to put aside enmity and reconnect with each other
as Jacob Carter did? And, lest we forget, might we doom a society by bypassing Gate
network protocols to get a lock? Okay, maybe not that one.
Each week we are invited to ponder what other worlds might be, through an allegorical
lens — through the eyes of SG-1. With each team member we may see a facet of
ourselves, and as we travel from planet to planet we grow with them. Then again,
you might not care about any of that. You may just want the action!
In the pages which follow, it's your turn to step through the gate. Expect to encounter
almost all of the facets you've grown to love about the show. The stories which
follow have been meticulously cultivated and considered to fit into the television
timeline, with new characters, races and planets mixed with some old ones to fill in
the world of Phoenix Site and beyond. Every new addition has been deliberate and
exhaustively argued over (believe me, I was there).
That being said, as with any work that is set within an existing continuity, we do
ask that you keep an open mind and give us some leeway in a couple of places. As
gamers, and more importantly, as fans ourselves, we believe it will make your play
time all the more enjoyable.
You've watched the show, so you're trained for this. Phoenix Site is in your capable
hands.
Good luck, and godspeed.
-David Read

When a player character tries to perform certain

CH 3: Races
Aturen
The Aturen, newly created for this game, are, to
most, a newfound race hailing from an ancient
civilization that lived in seclusion for tens of
thousands of years. Their species was once similar
to humanity, in trying to aggressively colonize
their world, and their Great Houses warred over
resources. This all came to an end when the Nox
revealed themselves to the Aturen and aspired to
teach them a better way. The Aturen, weary of
the conflicts that had too long occupied them,
were grateful for the Nox’s assistance and with
their help started a path towards enlightenment.
The Aturen dedicated themselves to studying the
great philosophy of peace and non-interference
that the Nox live by, though they are far from
perfect students. The Houses of the Aturen do
their best to settle their differences through debate
and their Parliament. Some Aturen have continued
to practice the martial ways of their ancestors.
They have not needed to engage in combat with
others since the Nox came and uplifted their
species, but they train and practice in case the
day comes when it is needed.
Using a gift from the Nox to shield their homeworld
from prying eyes, the Aturen were spared from the
ravages of the System Lords until recently when a
Tok’ra scout ship crash landed on a moon in their
solar system. Unwilling to leave the Tok’ra agent
to die, the Aturen broke their promise of non-
interference and took up the struggle against the
Goa’uld. Now the Aturen are preparing for war,
while the Nox silently look on as their children join
the struggle to free the galaxy from oppression.
The Aturen have allied themselves with the Tau’ri
and their alliance at Phoenix Site, and though
they do not have much to offer militarily, they
have pledged the full support of their science
and engineering breakthroughs.
Their society is not organized by nationality but by
which House an Aturen belongs to. Though there
are thousands of smaller Houses spread across
Atura, there are 5 Great Houses which control
most of Aturen society. Each is based around
their own interpretation of the Creed, which is
the philosophy based around the teachings that
the Nox tried to impart to the Aturen. The Great
Houses have been at peace with each other for
centuries, though as the Aturen open themselves
up to the galaxy, once more old feuds have
reawakened the bitter enmity between them. For
now, they have kept their focus on their conflict
with the System Lords, but the Nox fear for what
will become of their children as they stray further
away from their teachings.

CH 3: Races
Human
Life on Earth began in the primordial oceans,
slowly evolving into the upright biped of the
modern era. Millennia ago, the Goa’uld System
Lord Ra arrived on Earth and used his technology to
fool the citizens of Ancient Egypt into worshiping
him as a god. Ra was eventually forced to leave
Earth after his slaves revolted. By then he had
exported millions of his followers off-world. The
humans were so useful to the System Lords, they
bred them for use as hosts for the Goa’uld, and
to seed various worlds throughout the galaxy.
Little more than tools of the Goa’uld, the
transplanted humans had no opportunity to revive
their native culture and often lived knowing only
submission to their overlord. Some planets had
little value to the Goa’uld after the establishment
of human settlements and these supplicants were
left to fend for themselves, often thriving as their
natural curiosity and drive were left unchecked.
On Earth humans made their first unescorted
journey into the greater Milky Way when the
ancient Stargate was uncovered, almost ten
millennia after the first humans were enslaved.
Under the direction of the United States Air Force,
special teams were sent through the Stargate on
exploratory missions. Even after so many years
apart, the Tau’ri found other humans who were
virtually indistinguishable from themselves. The
members of SG-1 witnessed the cruelty and
tyranny of the Goa’uld and were not content to
simply explore, but instead work to liberate the
oppressed.
HUMAN WORLDS
Human life in the galaxy evolved on Earth and
was distributed over thousands of years by the
System Lords. The Jaffa, who were created from
genetically-modified humans, recognized these
first humans from their folklore as the “Tau’ri,” a
name meaning “The people of Earth.” Planets with
major free human civilizations currently known to
Stargate Command include the following:
Abydos (Undefined): The first planet where
human life was observed outside of Earth’s
solar system. Abydos is the first planet visited
by the Tau’ri under the auspices of the Stargate
Command.
Argos (P3X-8596): Argos is populated by bronze-
age humans experimented on by a System Lord
to live accelerated lives but, the SGC was able to
produce a cure.

pages.text:
CH 3: Races
Jaffa
At first glance, Jaffa appear as their ancestors
did when they were taken from their homes in
Ancient Egypt – strong, capable, and proud. But
like their forebears, the Jaffa live in subjugation.
When the first human devotees were taken to the
Goa’uld Queen on Dakara, she saw great potential
in them – as incubators for her children. There
the Queen twisted the human genome to leave
Jaffa hosts reliant on the Goa’uld for survival.
As children, Jaffa live normally. However, the
Goa’uld Queen engineered a fatal failure into their
immune system that is triggered during the Age of
Prata (roughly, the time of puberty), thus requiring
a symbiote be implanted. The strongest stock are
chosen for the Prim’ta ceremony. During this rite,
an abdominal pouch is opened in the Jaffa, and
their first symbiote is implanted. Within hours,
the child’s natural immune system is permanently
destroyed and replaced by the larval Goa’uld.
Despite their co-dependence, a Jaffa cannot
directly communicate with the symbiote within.
The only form of communication is through
Kelno’reem. This ritual deep meditation allows the
symbiote to heal and cleanse the host’s body. For
most Jaffa, this process is subconscious, although
a few speak on a more direct level. Almost any
illness or injury can be healed during this process.
The larval Goa’uld release naquadah into a Jaffa’s
bloodstream, granting the ability to control certain
Goa’uld technology and also sense the presence
of nearby naquadah.
Fueled by biological manipulation, the Jaffa
become fast and strong while their symbiote
uses their body to grow. Male Jaffa typically serve
the Goa’uld Armies, while female Jaffa remain
on their homeworld, ready to defend it from
outside forces. When a prim’ta matures, it must
be removed from the pouch and implanted in a
host. The Jaffa must be implanted with a new
symbiote, within a few hours, in order to avoid
death.
SYMBIOTES & HUMANS
The Goa’uld have a method for creating an
incubation pouch in humans. In this case,
the installation of the symbiote immediately
represses the natural immune system and
grants the regenerative abilities of a Jaffa. If
a Tau’ri with an abdominal pouch is healed
with a sarcophagus, the pouch and stomach
wounds will be healed. If such resources are
not available, from then on the recipient will
be dependent upon a symbiote or Tretonin
like all other Jaffa.

pages.title: Races
pages.text:
CH 3: Races
Tok’ra
The Tok’ra are a specific family of Goa’uld created
by the Goa’uld Queen Egeria. In opposition to
the tyranny of the System Lord Ra, she instilled
compassion in the genetic memory of her Prim’ta
and named them the Tok’ra – a name meaning
“against Ra.” In retaliation for the creation of the
Tok’ra, System Lord Ra had Queen Egeria removed
from her host and imprisoned for thousands of
years, leaving the Tok’ra without any new prim’ta.
Queen Egeria was discovered on the planet Pangar
where new prim’ta were used by locals to create
Tretonin, though she died soon after the SG-1
team obtained samples of the drug. These samples
would lead to the eventual invention of synthetic
Tretonin for the Jaffa. While Queen Egeria left
the Jaffa with the means to escape Goa’uld
domination, her greatest weapon against them,
the Tok’ra, will eventually become extinct without
her, as they cannot create new larval Goa’uld.
Tok’ra are unwilling to enslave their hosts and
believe they should live communally, sharing one
body. While Goa’uld take their hosts in whatever
manner may be convenient, Tok’ra prefer to enter
through a host’s mouth, thereby minimizing any
exterior deformation. Tok’ra may choose a host
based on convenience, curiosity, or kindness.
After a Tok’ra has been removed from a host,
there are no adverse impacts, although the host
will continue to have naquadah in their blood
and be able to sense it nearby. Most Tok’ra
technology relies on the presence of naquadah
in the bloodstream to activate.
The youngest Tok’ra are from Pangar and were
created with a flaw that prevents the production
of Tretonin, which also resulted in the loss of their
genetic memory. Some have chosen to remain on
Pangar and continue the life they built with their
hosts before the arrival of SG-1; however more
found that the Goa’uld are a foe worth fighting.
To this day, though they are of the same species,
Tok’ra do not identify as Goa’uld and consider
the Tau’ri allies against the System Lords. When
General Loyer set up the Phoenix Site, he
approached the Tok’ra for assistance. Seeing this
as an opportunity to weaken the Goa’uld System
Lords, several Tok’ra agreed to lend their aid in
intelligence, logistics, and even as operatives on
Phoenix Site teams.

CH 3: Races
Unas
The Unas evolved on the same homeworld as
the Goa’uld and became their first hosts. With
natural strength and regenerative abilities which
could be further enhanced, they served the System
Lords as enforcers and laborers. Use of the Unas
quickly fell out of favor with the System Lords
when the introduction of human hosts provided
a wider range of vocalization and higher manual
dexterity. Humans quickly replaced them as the
preferred host; however, primal Goa’uld still infest
the waters of P3X-888, threatening resident Unas.
While the Unas lack the vocal range of humans,
they are capable of mimicking some words and
phrases, and their language is not so divergent
as to prevent communication. Many linguists,
building on the works of Dr. Daniel Jackson, have
learned enough of the language to communicate
with them. Through the concerted efforts of
various Stargate teams, an alliance with several
tribes of Unas from P3X-888 was forged, and the
brightest Unas – those who have shown promise
in understanding the Tau’ri language – have joined
the Phoenix Site in the fight against the Goa’uld.
Those who remain behind keep the old ways of
their ancestors. They form small tribal communities
which are led by a single dominant Unas, typically
a male. Younger Unas are given tasks to complete
as a rite of passage, which often involves venturing
forth into the world to provide for the tribe. Even
with the improved communication between Unas
and Stargate Command, little is known about the
internal structure of the tribes, but in contrast
to their beastly appearance, the Unas show high
levels of empathy and creativity.
Unas are reptilian in nature, with bulky bodies,
large hands, and green blood. While they have
greater regenerative abilities than a Tau’ri, they
are not invulnerable and can succumb to high
amounts of damage. They do not carry any
naquadah in their system and neither do the
primal Goa’uld threatening their planet.

Subject: Speech by Emissary Tolii to Tok’ra Council
[Transcriber’s note: The original recording on crystal]
The Phoenix Alliance is all of us. Each species has something unique to offer, be it superior
technology and knowledge, or relentless bravado. We need each other if we are to defeat
the Goa’uld. We need the Phoenix Alliance. And, by extension, we need Haven. It is on this
topic I speak to you today.
Haven is not a town as the Tok’ra would build it. One might argue it is barely a “town” at
all, but rather a thrown-together collection of disparate structures. Yet, one cannot deny the
value inherent to its purpose. Haven feeds the Phoenix base, and it provides us with leisure Introduction
pursuits when off duty. More importantly, it fosters the unity the Alliance needs. We cannot
extend one hand in friendship, and the other to ward off overtures. We stand together, Character
or we do not. Time spent in Haven may not have given me a newfound appreciation of Creation
Tau’ri pursuits, but it has granted me deeper insights. Ambassador Kelley taught me how to
play pool, and I recognize its social function even if I do not enjoy the game itself. Several
Racesconversations with Ry’anna allowed me to better understand the Jaffa’s anger at their
enslavement by the Goa’uld, and the sadness on the loss of their own culture. Haven has
been crucial in forging these new and closer relationships. Origins
Thus I stand before you, requesting you appoint me to the Council of Haven. The Council
serves as an advisory body to the leader of Haven. This affords the people of the Alliance Classes
more say in the town, and therefore more opportunities to integrate their cultural practices.
Let us forge a collective future, as well as a common foe against which to fight. To wit, Equipment

appointed a councilor, but I believe they lean toward Hatana, who was one of their first
explorers to make contact with the Alliance. Feats

Using Abilitywise. The Tau’ri have invested more resources and people in the Phoenix base than any other
Scoresspecies. It seems appropriate the ultimate decisions on their fates lie in their own hands. I
also believe we could do worse than ambassador Kelley, who has shown herself to possess
more tact than many other Tau’ri. She has already stated her welcome of a new council, Missions
and I believe her to be sincere.

Program Brief
Subject: HOME Initiative
To: General P.K. Loyer
From: A’bebe, Head of HOME Initiative
It is so good to meet you all. I am A’bebe. My planet is ruled by a false god named Ba’al.
He is a cruel man, using torture and biological weapons to keep my people in check. He
is callous, sacrificing us by the thousands to weaken his enemies. He is also common, just
one of many self-styled gods laying claim to the galaxy.
My family fled Ba’al when I was young; I had just received my prim’ta. This was a time of
considerable uncertainty for us. Ba’al was cruel, but he told us other people were even
worse. He said they would strike us down without mercy to kill the prim’ta inside us. My
family rejected his doctrine of fear and made a leap of faith. They believed there were people
in the galaxy who would not condemn us for the place of our birth, but instead see us for
who we were and help us. My family was right, and I grew up in freedom.
Freedom is the most precious gift in the universe, but it means nothing if not shared. Unless
all slaves of the Goa’uld are free, none of us are. We rise together! So I joined the rebellion
when I was old enough. I spent my entire adult life bringing the families of rebel Jaffa to
safety, out of the reach of false gods who would seek retribution. My combat skills are
subpar for a Jaffa, I admit, but I have a keen nose for people; Smugglers who will not sell
you out, Guards who will not reveal you, and now you, the Tau’ri. You are good people,
brave people. You gave me the means to found this initiative. We’ve named it HOME, for
that is what you and I will bring to the people of the Milky Way: a new home.

Blue (M3D-689) is a small moon in close orbit around a large
gas giant. The people of Blue are Tau’ri descendants, and I’d put
their development comparable to early twentieth-century America. Introduction
The Aschen do not use electricity, but harvest gas to serve as fuel.
They’ve offered to aid the people of Blue in their mining operations. Character
The Aschen also provide an inoculation against “Blue Sickness” Creation
caused by too much exposure to the gas. The local people have not
yet experienced any ill side-effects and were lining up around the Races
block to receive the immunization. They believe Blue Sickness is
the one thing standing between themselves and harvesting the full Origins
riches of the fuel, and anticipate industrial leaps when they can ramp
up their mining operation. While the injection is not mandatory, it Classes
has become a prerequisite for working in the gas mines, which is
the largest source of employment on Blue. No one forced us, but Equipment
locals did look askew when we declined the drug. The Aschen
Featsthemselves did not seem to care much. I suppose there’s a tipping
point where it doesn’t matter if everyone is sterilized or just a large
Using Abilityenough portion of the populace.
I was able to speak to the Aschen envoys at this time, who let a Scores
few things slip while explaining the vaccine to me. They hail from Missions
a prosperous world and travel the galaxy to share their riches with
other people. Clearly, the latter is a lie. Their Confederation, once Encounters

of interstellar travel. They now count six worlds as part of their STARGATE

they have moved on. Even so, I support Captain Rodriguez in her
desire to stop these people. Their actions are an affront to everything
moral and good. They are despicable.

BEING A SPOTLIGHT IN ACTION ENCOUNTERS GATEMASTER
Paradoxically, action encounters are both the easiest and most difficult situations to balance
spotlight time, depending on your Phoenix team’s makeup. Teams that have similar combat
Life Forms
potency across all characters pose significantly fewer troubles than those with broader abilities.
When the group contains characters who are equally prepared (or unprepared) for combat,
Appendix
then there is little a GM must do to ensure that every character gets a moment of spotlight
during a fight. The base turn order, a variety of combat scenarios, and critical hits, all work
together to keep things interesting and give each character a little moment to shine.
However, most groups won’t be comprised of two soldiers, a scout, and a medic. Often, the
players will all want to play various classes and pursue different options post level 5. To ensure
that every player has a moment to shine during the action encounters, the GM will need to
occasionally employ the following tools:
• Employ non-attack rolls, such as science or engineering checks, to manipulate the battlefield
by hacking turrets, retracting drawbridges, shutting blast doors, or creating makeshift cover.
• Create alternate objectives to simply defeating all the enemies present, like convincing
an asset to flee with you, deciphering alien text, or repairing a damage DHD before enemy
reinforcements arrive.
• Include weaker enemies who move on the non-combat focused PCs aggressively, while
forcing the combat focused PCs to deal with more dangerous threats.

on a frequent basis, either as part of a one-
off story or as a recurring ally or villain. One
of the easiest ways to create a new race is
to use the abilities found in the Beasts entry

established racial abilities, modify them to
